events.title: Browserify first released
events.summary: James Halliday published Browserify on February 3, 2011 — a bundler that let browsers use Node-style `require()` for npm modules.
events.about: Browserify walks `require()` dependencies and packs them into one file for the browser — the first mainstream way to compose npm packages on the client. It paved the way for webpack, Rollup, and the modern frontend toolchain. Example: `browserify main.js -o bundle.js` ships lodash and your app code to static hosting.

narrative.whyChosen: Browserify proved npm modules could run in browsers, not just on servers.
narrative.whyImportant: It launched the module-bundler era that reshaped how JavaScript apps are built and deployed.
narrative.problemSolved: Browsers had no native module system; developers could not reuse the growing npm ecosystem client-side.

events.title: Travis CI launched
events.summary: Sven Fuchs introduced Travis CI on February 5, 2011 — a hosted continuous integration service built for the Ruby and open-source community.
events.about: Travis connected GitHub repos to build workers — push a commit, see green or red in minutes. A `.travis.yml` defined language, test commands, and matrix builds. It made CI badges on READMEs normal and inspired CircleCI, GitHub Actions, and the SaaS CI wave.

narrative.whyChosen: Travis CI brought push-button hosted CI to open-source projects on GitHub.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved developers would trust cloud CI for every commit, not just release builds.
narrative.problemSolved: Self-hosted Jenkins was heavy for small teams; OSS needed free, Git-native automation.

events.title: Ninja build system open-sourced
events.summary: Evan Martin open-sourced Ninja on February 6, 2011 — a minimal build system focused on maximum compile speed.
events.about: Ninja executes build graphs generated by CMake, Meson, or GN — no string manipulation, just fast dependency tracking and parallel compilation. Chrome's Linux builds dropped from 10 seconds to under one second for incremental rebuilds. Example: CMake emits `build.ninja`; `ninja -C build` compiles only changed translation units.

narrative.whyChosen: Ninja became the low-level backend that made large C++ projects rebuild in seconds.
narrative.whyImportant: It separated build configuration (CMake/Meson) from execution, setting the pattern for modern native builds.
narrative.problemSolved: Make-based incremental builds were too slow for million-line codebases like Chromium.
